Gnorp Apologue is a strange game. I'd recommend it because it's still fun at the end of the day, but a lot of its features are very contradictory in a way that points to weird game design. 

The best example of this is how many things increase how far things launch and treat this as a good feature. It comes with a lot of upgrades. You might be tempted to think that this is good because it makes shards (the currency that spills from the rock) easier to collect, sometimes outright dropping them into the stash. Certain units shove them forward, many upgrades to statuses increase the knockback of said status (the first unlocked talent exclusively does this), and it all seems pointed toward making collection easier... but the game isn't about collection.

Collection is a means to an end, it increases your talent point gain, but the goal is to make the pile tall, not wide.

Only a few hours in, but I can already say that this is my favorite incremental idler game I've played, out of maybe 7 or 8 games.  Everything you do in the game is reflected in the actual visual, instead of just a progress bar with an absurdly large number to trick you into feeling like you've done something. The Gnorps are fun to watch, and it really feels like you are helping mastermind some whacky excavation project. So much more satisfying than I thought it would be, and easily worth the time and money. It's also clear that the Devs care about the overall experience of the player instead of just using the game as a vehicle for a cashgrab.
Just get it.  100% would recommend.

Less an idle game about gradual linear progression, Gnorp Apologue rewards players who like to tinker with various builds.  It's a game about making the correct decisions, more than watching numbers go up.  There's no way to know how powerful an upgrade, effect, or unit will be without just trying it.

After grinding for a while and repeatedly creating failed builds, I realized that trial-and-error, min-max gaming is not what I'm looking for right now.  I looked up a guide. Just by following its list of recommended starting abilities, and mostly ignoring the step-by-step instructions, I was able to win a run in less than an hour.

Fine.

[h1]Short Review[/h1]

(the) Gnorp Apologue is a surprisingly polished incremental game that knows how to keep you hooked without burning out its welcome. The pixel art is genuinely charming, the music fits the vibe perfectly, and the addictive loop of watching your little Gnorps do their thing is oddly satisfying. The talent system has some dead weight in it, and the late-game grind for Zybellium can hit a frustrating wall if you're not managing your resources right. But if you're looking for a short, sweet incremental that actually has an endpoint in sight, this one delivers.

[h1]Full Review[/h1]

I have a soft spot for incremental games, and (the) Gnorp Apologue caught my eye with its pixel art and the inexplicable charm of watching tiny creatures do inexplicable things. I went in not knowing what to expect and came out having completed the whole thing without ever feeling like I was
A simple, fun, and thoughtful game that I thoroughly enjoyed! We need more games like this and Tower Wizard.

One must imagine Gnorpyphus happy

I love Gnorp, I love seeing my little Gnorplings hard at work at their Gnorpyphean task of destroying the evil rock. 

"(the) Gnorp Apologue" Is a 21st century artistic masterpiece. The soundtrack, albeit repetitive works in the games favour. You will come no closer to a video game representation of Camus's phrase "One must imagine Sisyphus happy". After the first hour of Gnorping you come to realise that the goal was never to destroy the rock, it was never to "beat the game". The goal was for the player to find joy in the struggle. 

Although technically an idle game it stands out from many other, that being its artstyle. The game is just nice looking at, seeing your Gnorplings with different hats, seeing their houses stacked on high with a flower pot or two, to witness them working is like observing an ant farm.

For what it is, it is highly enjoyable

This game is really fun. Great time kill. A lot of incremental games like this are designed to have you always chasing power creep. So while I appreciate seeing an incremental game that has a definitive "I beat the game" point, I do wish there was more content. Not because the content in the game is lacking or bad, but because it's so good I wish there was more.

A linear incremental idle game with charming pixel art and satisfying progression. I've unlocked about half the skill tree so far and completed the base game mode.

But here's the catch - pick the wrong upgrades or mismanage your resources, and you can genuinely break your run. No exaggeration. One bad choice and you're stuck restarting.

It's a polished, addictive experience with great visuals and a relaxing vibe. Just don't expect deep build variety or endless content - it's pretty linear and short.

This was a very interesting experience. At some point you realise that some talents are total garbage and you need to learn which ones work and which do not as you can't tell from just looking at them.
I tried building a fire build expecting something big to just to be very disappointed by it.
In general, this was very interesting experience and fun to figure things out.

I'll leave this review short. For a game I bought for $3, its worth every penny. In fact I would've probably paid up to $15. This is a fun little game with an addicting gameplay loop.

Pros
- Affordable
- Accessible
- Nostalgic

Cons
- Graphics are a bit simple and I wish it had more cinematics and special effects.
- The progression can be a little slow at times without a lot of ways to progress, often leading to me pressing prestige. (I'd recommend adding a way to reassign a Gnorp).

Overall, just buy it, or make a footcam account if you cant afford it yet.

I'm sorry man, I know it's an idler, but I got sucked in to trying to complete it so I could uninstall it once I got the prestige points I needed. It perpetually dangles the win state in front of you while pulling the rug out from multiple angles to the point that you need to have a meta build and know every mechanic and late-game element so that you can finally reach the end. Combine this with the experience of sunk cost after having already dumped hours into it and the win that seems just out of reach and I personally come away with a bad feeling. It reminded me of how claw machines make children feel, or how slots and blackjack make gamblers feel. I'm sure a lot of people enjoy it and will make fun of me for this but the mechanics for me felt predatory in the end. I guess it turns out the game had played me.

The Gnorp Apologue is essentially a guess & check where you synergize upgrades you select at the very start of a run.

Instead of constantly upgrading, you just have to find the correct synergy to win.  Since these major upgrades are locked behind unlocking prestige tokens (which are set behind an arbitrary production amount), there is a [i]very[/i] artificial time gate in the way of this.

You will not have the power to complete the game until you have access to the final set of upgrades, and that's going to take a while of guess & checking to get enough prestige points.
